lang.name: English
meta.title: GTNH Crop Breeding Planner (CropsNH)
meta.description: Plan CropsNH breeding in GregTech: New Horizons 2.9. Tick the seeds you hold and see what you can make next, the odds for any pair of parents, and the route to a goal crop. Read straight out of the mod.
rail.title: Your seeds
rail.progressLabel: Share of all crops you hold
rail.legendSub: needs a specific block under the soil
rail.legendBreeder: only from the Crop Breeder, never from a stick
rail.legendNone: no route at all, not even the machine
manage.about: Your ticks live in this browser. The hosted page and a local copy keep separate stores - use this box to move the list between them.
manage.dlnote: This page runs in a sandboxed frame, so it cannot write files. Use Copy and paste the text somewhere safe - the offline copy of this page can download instead.
bio.intro: Type the biome you are standing in and it says whether this crop grows there with no water and no fertiliser. It filters the two lists below at the same time.
bio.found: That biome, with no water and no fertiliser
bio.row: ${n} tags match · rainfall ${BIOMES[b].rain} · the biome adds ${give} · Nutrient Score ${score}, and it needs more than ${limit}
bio.roofOnly: grows outdoors, not under a roof
bio.noneFound: No biome in this pack has a name like that.
bio.noneHere: Nothing in this list matches that name.
help.title: It won't grow without help
help.about: With no water and no fertiliser this crop needs more than ${limit} Nutrient Score to grow at all, and an empty crop stick under open sky is worth 7 before the biome adds anything. Below that it makes no progress whatsoever, and a plant making no progress rolls its resistance every tick and eventually falls sick. Filling either the water or the fertiliser is worth 10 and usually fixes it.
help.open: Will not grow in ${open.length} of the ${Object.keys(BIOMES).length} biomes:
help.roofed: Grows outdoors, but will not grow under a roof or underground, in ${roofed.length}:
help.none: With no water and no fertiliser it still grows anywhere in this pack.
foot.data: Extracted from the bytecode of cropsnh-2.0.101.jar, as shipped in GTNH 2.9 - recipes, pools, soils, sub-soils and light requirements come straight out of MutationLoader, CropLoader and SubSoilRequirementLoader, not from a wiki. Nothing else in the pack registers crops with CropsNH, so the list above is the whole set rather than a selection.
foot.privacy: Your ticks are stored in this browser and nowhere else. The page makes no external requests and works offline - move a list between copies from Manage list in the sidebar.
msg.badFormat: Unrecognised format - paste a code from this tool.
msg.noneKnown: Found no known crops in that - nothing was changed.
msg.loadedUndo: · Undo is at the top of this panel
msg.cleared: Cleared ${undoState.length} crops - Undo is right above.
msg.clipboardBlocked: Clipboard is blocked - the box is selected, press Ctrl+C.
msg.downloadRefused: The browser refused the download - use Copy instead.
empty.tickFirst: Tick off what you have in the rail on the left.
empty.newHere: New here? Read the Quick start
empty.readyNone:
No new recipe is fully covered by this set.
Try One parent short or the Pool roulette.
empty.nearNone: No recipe is exactly one parent away.
ready.note: Recipes where you already hold every parent. Put the parents around a double crop stick, and make sure the ground under the stick satisfies the result's requirements - otherwise the attempt is discarded silently. Click a card to mark what you are building and it stays at the front; click it again to set it aside at the end. Anything you have not ruled on sits in between, which is also where a new recipe turns up.
near.note: One crop short, shown in rust. Click a name to see where the missing parent comes from, or the card itself to mark it - once for the front, twice to set it aside at the end.
pool.note: What can come out of a double crop stick between two crops that are at least 80% grown. Figures are the chance per successful breeding attempt, and one fires on roughly every third growth tick. The same crop twice is allowed, and is the most common setup.
pool.gain: ${pct(o.gain)} chance at one of ${o.newCount} crops you do not have yet.
pool.noGain: This pair gives you nothing new - you already have every possible result.
pool.cloneSame: both neighbours are the same crop
pool.recipeNote: This pair has a specific recipe, so the mutation branch goes there instead of drawing from a pool.
pool.recipeTie: ${o.det.length} recipes match and the engine picks one at random, hence ${pct(0.5 / o.det.length)} each.
pool.recipeFallback: If the recipe's conditions are not met, that half falls back to a pool draw instead.
pool.noPoolSame: ${esc(A.name)} belongs to no pool - that crop is recipe-only.
pool.noPoolShared: This pair shares neither a pool nor a recipe.
pool.noPoolTail: The mutation branch always fails - you will only ever get copies of the parents.
pool.sharedSame: Two identical crops match every pool ${esc(A.name)} belongs to: ${poolTxt}.
pool.drawNote: The pool is drawn uniformly - a small pool is worth as much as a large one, it just spreads over fewer crops.
pool.blockNote: Top block is the one directly under the crop stick, under block is one deeper. A result whose ground you have not built simply never gets planted, so setting those two blocks up for the crop you actually want quietly removes most of this table.
best.title: Best pairs from your seeds
best.note: Ranked by the total chance of a crop you do not have yet. Click a pair to load its full breakdown.
best.pickFirst: Pick two crops above - or tick off what you have on the left and I will rank the best pairs.
best.none: No pair from your seeds yields anything new. You need a crop from outside the current set.
path.intro: This works out a chain of recipes from the crops you already hold to one you want.
path.tickFirst: Tick off what you have in the rail on the left first.
path.tickWhy: With nothing ticked there is no starting point, so every goal would come back unreachable.
path.note: A chain of recipes from what you hold to the crop you want. It only follows exact recipes, so a crop that comes out of a pool draw will not have a route here even though you can still get it.
path.groupBlocked: Needs something you do not have yet (${blockedOpts.length})
path.pickGoal: Pick a goal. ${reachableOpts.length} crops are reachable from what you hold right now.
path.noneReachable:
Nothing is reachable by recipe from your current set yet.
Tick off more of what you actually own, or use the Pool roulette to find a first new crop.
path.noRecipe: ${esc(nm(target))} has no recipe at all. It only ever comes out of a pool draw or from the world, so there is no chain to follow. See the Pool roulette.
path.blockedBy: ${esc(nm(target))} cannot be reached by recipe yet. It is made by ${made}, with the parts you are missing in rust:
path.stateReachable: reachable by recipe, set it as the goal first
path.stateInPools: no route yet, but it is in ${inPools} pool${inPools > 1 ? "s" : ""}
path.poolNote: To draw this crop, use two seeds from any one of these pools. The same seed twice is allowed.
path.stateNoPool: no route yet and it is in no pool, so it needs its own recipe chain
path.stateWild: has no recipe, you have to find it in the world
card.markTitle: Click to mark this as what you are building
card.markedTitle: Marked as what you are building - click again to set it aside
card.parkedTitle: Set aside and sorted to the end - click to bring it back
drawer.poolIntro: Mutation pool with ${members.length} crops in it. Two parents that both belong to this pool can draw any one of them, each equally likely. You already hold ${mine.length}.
drawer.poolAllOwned: You have every crop in this pool.
drawer.poolNoneMine: None of these are ticked yet.
drawer.stack: Crop stick on top, top block directly under it, under block one deeper.
drawer.pairSelfTitle: Set this crop as both parents and open the Pool roulette
drawer.poolsNote: Any two parents that share one of these can draw this crop at random. Open a pool to see everything else in it.
drawer.noPools: None - this crop can only be obtained from a recipe.
drawer.noRecipePools: Only ever from a pool draw, see the ${c.pools.length} pool${c.pools.length > 1 ? "s" : ""} above.
drawer.noRecipeWild: Not from a pool either, so this one is found in the world.
drawer.altSeed: Alternate seed. An ordinary item plants this crop straight onto a crop stick, at 1/1/1 and already analysed, so no cross is needed to get one. NEI lists which item under Alternate Seeds.
drawer.altSeedItems: Alternate seed: ${items}. Put one straight onto a crop stick and the crop is standing there at 1/1/1, already analysed. No breeding involved.

tips.g1.lead: Three setups that fail silently. None of them show an error.
tips.g1.i1: Farmland is not dirt. This is the single most common one. Tilling flips a block between two requirements that share nothing at all: ${Object.values(C).filter(c => topParts(c).join() === "farmland").length} crops want farmland and refuse plain dirt, while ${Object.values(C).filter(c => topParts(c).join() === "dirtGrass").length} want dirt or grass and nothing else. Check the top block on the card against the block actually under your stick.
tips.g1.i1w: The two soil lists have no block in common, so a hoe turns a valid spot into an invalid one in whichever direction you were not thinking about. Mind the lookalikes: the farmland list also holds Magic Bees' enchanted earth, Random Things' tilled fertilized dirt and Ztones' clean dirt - and that last one looks exactly like plain dirt while counting as farmland. The dirt list is vanilla dirt and grass plus Chisel's dirt block.
tips.g1.i2: The top block is right and the one underneath is missing. That second block is checked when the mutation happens, not only afterwards for growing. Without it the roll is discarded and nothing is reported. Anything marked ◆ in the seed list needs one.
tips.g1.i2w: SubSoilRequirement reports onlyPreventsHarvest() = false, so the pre-planting check rejects the result outright. It also implements the breeding-requirement interface, whose check simply delegates to the growth check.
tips.g1.i3: Breaking a plant below resistance 31 can destroy the seed. The seed comes back on a roll against resistance, so at 20 you lose it about one time in three. At 31 it is guaranteed. Harvest for produce instead, or push resistance up before you start pulling plants.
tips.g1.i3w: getSeedDrop() returns null unless passesResistanceCheck() passes, which is resistance > random(0…30). Only 31 beats every roll. The left-click path calls doPlayerHarvest(player, true), which clears the stick either way - so a failed roll takes the plant with it.
tips.g2.lead: A double crop stick keeps trying for as long as it stands there. Each attempt is independent of the last.
tips.g2.i1: A double crop stick only tries to breed on roughly one growth tick in three. Everything below is the chance per attempt, not per tick.
tips.g2.i1w: attemptBreeding() opens with a roll against the Breeding Chance config (default 3) and returns immediately on two out of three results.
tips.g2.i2: Each attempt splits 50/50. Half the time the stick copies a neighbour, half the time it mutates. Getting copies of the parents over and over is the expected result, not bad luck.
tips.g2.i2w: getBreedingResult() begins with a 50/50 draw. One result takes the cloning path, which keeps only neighbours grown enough to cross, picks one at random and replants its crop. The other takes the mutation path. If no neighbour is grown enough, the cloning path falls through to the mutation path instead.
tips.g2.i3: A parent does not have to be fully grown. Once a plant is 80% grown it already counts, on both paths. The last fifth of the bar changes nothing about breeding - it only decides what you get when you harvest.
tips.g2.i3w: attemptBreeding() gathers every neighbour and drops only the empty sticks and the weeds - it never calls getMatureNeighbours(). The growth test comes later and once per path: cloning keeps the neighbours that pass canCross(), mutation those that pass canBreed(). Both compare getGrowthPercent() against a threshold read off the crop, and CropCard returns 0.8f for each. A crop whose threshold is negative is dropped outright, which is why Primordial Berry can never be a parent at a crop stick.
tips.g2.i4: If the result cannot be planted on that spot, the roll is discarded. No message, no half-grown plant. The stick stays empty and tries again later, and that same tick still rolls its usual small chance of a weed.
tips.g2.i4w: attemptBreeding() plants only when both isValidSoilForCrop() and wouldCropBeAbleToGrow() pass for the result. Otherwise it returns false - the same signal a missed breeding roll gives - and that is exactly what lets the weed spawn roll run on the same tick.
tips.g3.lead: You cannot change the odds of a roll, but you can change which results are possible.
tips.g3.i1: Two of the same crop can never produce a recipe result, but they match every pool that crop belongs to. That is the widest range of results available from one pair.
tips.g3.i1w: The recipe lookup runs the parents through a .distinct() filter first, so two identical crops collapse into one entry and fail the "at least two parents" check. The pool lookup has no such filter, so both entries survive and every pool containing that crop matches.
tips.g3.i2: Two different crops that share a recipe will give that recipe, not a random pool result. Pools only get a look in if the recipe's own conditions are not satisfied.
tips.g3.i2w: getBreedingResult() asks for matching recipes first. If there are any, one is drawn at random and its conditions checked; only when that check fails does it drop through to the pool draw.
tips.g3.i3: A small pool is worth exactly as much as a large one. The pool is picked first and the crop second, so a 7-crop pool splits its share of the odds seven ways and a 50-crop pool splits the same share fifty ways.
tips.g3.i3w: The matching pools are collected into a list and one is chosen with a flat random index, then a member of that pool is chosen the same way. Pool size never weights either draw.
tips.g3.i4: A pool only counts if at least two of the parents belong to it.
tips.g3.i4w: MutationPool.isMatch() walks the parent list counting members and returns true the moment the counter reaches two.
tips.g3.i5: A third crop beside the stick can block the recipe you wanted. Keep only the parents you need next to a breeding stick. A spare grown plant of another crop can stop a recipe you already have both parents for, with no indication that it did.
tips.g3.i5w: The crops present are sorted by internal id and walked strictly index by index. MutationMap.findMatches() reads entry i, and if there is no branch for it, it returns rather than skipping ahead - so a recipe fires only when its own sorted parents are the leading entries of that list. With A, B and C grown around one stick, a recipe for A + C is never found, because after A the walk demands B. Neighbours below their breeding threshold are filtered out beforehand, so an immature plant cannot block anything.
tips.g3.i6: Use the ground to narrow the pool. Build it for one specific crop and most of the pool cannot be planted there at all, so the few that can appear far more often. This does not raise the overall rate, it only changes which results are possible.
tips.g3.i6w: This is the same wouldCropBeAbleToGrow() check. Every requirement whose onlyPreventsHarvest() is false stops the result from being planted at all, and the attempt is discarded rather than substituted.
tips.g4.lead: Two blocks below the stick are checked, at different depths and against different lists.
tips.g4.i1: The top block is the one directly under the crop stick. The under block goes one deeper, two blocks below the stick and underneath the top block.
tips.g4.i1w: isValidSoilForCrop() reads the block at y - 1. SubSoilRequirement.getSubSoil() starts by doing y -= 2.
tips.g4.i2: Ore counts, not just the crafted block. A gold ore block under the soil works as well as a block of gold.
tips.g4.i2w: Each sub-soil carries a GregTech material, and the check accepts any block whose GregTech association is that material with the block prefix or any prefix starting with ore - so every ore variant counts, not only the storage block. GregTech's own ore blocks are matched straight off their material metadata.
tips.g4.i3: Light rules apply to mutation too. A crop that needs darkness will not appear in daylight under an open sky. Outdoors it only gets a chance at night; under a roof it works at any hour.
tips.g4.i3w: The requirement reads the actual light level at the stick rather than a sky-access flag, and the minimum and maximum light requirements both report onlyPreventsHarvest() = false, so they gate planting in exactly the same way the sub-soil does.
tips.g4.i4: A few crops accept several different top blocks - ${Object.values(C).filter(c => topParts(c).length > 1).length} of the ${Object.keys(C).length} - so a listing like "Stone / Dirt​/grass / Mycelium / Netherrack" means any one of them will do, not all four. Glowshroom is one of them. Every other crop accepts exactly one top block.
tips.g4.i4w: Those few come from soil lists that are unions of other lists rather than lists of blocks. netherMushroom is mushroom plus netherrack, and mushroom is itself stone plus dirt/grass plus mycelium. This page expands those unions instead of showing the internal name.
tips.g4.i5: The parents can stand on completely different ground than the breeding stick. Only the stick's own ground decides what may appear on it.
tips.g4.i5w: The soil and sub-soil checks are run against the coordinates of the breeding stick alone. Neighbours are read for their crop, their stats, how grown they are and whether their own stick still holds fertiliser - never for what they are standing on.
tips.g5.lead: Both feed a single number the game calls the Nutrient Score, and that number decides how fast anything grows - or whether it grows at all.
tips.g5.i1: A full water tank is worth +10 Nutrient Score, and so is full fertiliser. They add up rather than replace each other: a crop that is watered but not fertilised has half of what the pair is worth, and topping the fertiliser up as well is another 50% of growth speed. The base score is 5 and an open sky adds 2. These two tanks are the largest contribution you control.
tips.g5.i1w: The score is built as: base 5, plus up to 10 for water, plus up to 10 for fertiliser, plus 2 for sky access, plus whichever is larger of a humidity bonus (up to 14) or a liked-biome bonus (up to 28), for a ceiling of 55. Water and fertiliser count in tenths rounded up, so a single stored unit is already worth +1 and 100 gives the full 10.
tips.g5.i2: A higher-tier crop will simply refuse to grow on a dry stick - unless the biome is carrying it. The score a crop needs is twice its tier, and base plus open sky only reaches 7, which covers tier 3 and nothing above it. A wet or liked biome adds score whatever your tanks say, so the same crop that stalls in a desert can grow untended in a jungle.
tips.g5.i2w: Growth rate compares score × 5 against tier × 10, so the requirement is a score of twice the tier. Each point of that scaled difference adds 1% speed, or costs 4% below the line down to a floor of zero - and since one Nutrient Score point is five of them, a score point is worth +5% above the line and -20% below it. Measured against the same crop with both tanks full, in a biome giving no humidity or liked-biome bonus: a tier 3 crop on a dry stick runs at about half speed, a tier 5 at roughly a fifth, and a tier 8 does not grow at all.
tips.g5.i3: Keep both topped up all the time - every growth tick spends a point of each, so they drain constantly. Outdoors, rain refills water for free. Early on the easiest tool by far is the Watering Can from Extra Utilities: hold right-click over the patch and it keeps the whole thing wet.
tips.g5.i3w: The growth tick decrements the water and fertiliser stores by one each. Rain tops water up 11 points at a time, skipped if the store is already over 100 and capped at 101 - that extra point covers the same tick's own -1, so it settles at exactly 100. (Which tool you use is practical advice. How full you keep it is not: the score scales with the amount stored, so a nearly empty tank is not the same as a full one.)
tips.g5.i4: Before you can produce fertiliser yourself, buy it from a vending machine. It is the cheapest early supply, and a breeding farm consumes it constantly. It raises growth speed and protects your stats at the same time.
tips.g5.i4w: One store is read by two separate systems: the Nutrient Score takes up to 10 from it, and the stat roll uses it as the condition for clamping away negative results. (Where you buy it is practical advice, not a code detail.)
tips.g5.i5: The enriched versions are worth ten times as much per unit - that goes for fertiliser and for Weed-EX alike. Once you can make them, the same tank lasts ten times longer.
tips.g5.i5w: Fluids are registered with a potency value. Plain fertiliser is 1 and enriched fertiliser is 10; plain Weed-EX is 1 and GregTech's WeedEX9000 is 10.
tips.g5.i6: Distilled water hydrates twice as well as ordinary water, which matters once you are piping water to the crops.
tips.g5.i6w: The hydration registry gives ordinary water a potency of 1 and GregTech's distilled water a potency of 2.
tips.g6.lead: Growth, gain and resistance drift a little on every successful cross.
tips.g6.i1: Fertiliser in every parent stops stats from dropping. One parent running dry restores the negative half of the roll for all three stats.
tips.g6.i1w: Each stat rolls a change between the Breeding Range Low and High configs, -2 to +4 by default. Only when every counted parent still has fertiliser is a negative roll clamped to zero.
tips.g6.i2: The starting point is the average of the parents that actually counted - not of everything standing around the stick.
tips.g6.i2w: The average is taken over the filtered parent list: for a copy only the neighbours grown past their crossing threshold and holding the same crop, for a mutation only those past their breeding threshold whose crop is in the recipe's parents or the matched pool. An under-grown neighbour contributes nothing to the average, and its empty fertiliser tank is ignored as well. It is integer division, so fractions are lost each time.
tips.g7.lead: Weeds cannot destroy a grown crop. The risk is to the empty stick between the parents.
tips.g7.i1: Resistance 31 is total immunity, and it covers three separate checks: the plant cannot be overgrown, cannot fall sick, and cannot be trampled. Below 31 the chance of resisting a disease is resistance ÷ 31, so 20 gives about 65% and 25 about 81%. It is the most useful stat to max on anything you intend to leave standing.
tips.g7.i1w: The disease check is resistance > random(0…30), a uniform roll that a resistance of r wins r times out of 31 and that only 31 beats every time. The overgrowth path and the trample check each have their own explicit "resistance of 31 or more, do nothing" guard.
tips.g7.i3: Weeds never replace a grown crop. A weed beside a planted crop transfers disease instead, and that is what resistance blocks.
tips.g7.i3w: Weed planting has only two call sites in the whole mod, and both fire only on a stick holding no crop. When a spreading weed finds an occupied neighbour it calls the disease transfer instead.
tips.g7.i4: The empty stick in the middle is the vulnerable one. If a weed grows there, breeding stops completely. The parents are unaffected, but nothing more will be produced until you clear it.
tips.g7.i4w: An empty stick rolls the Weed Spawn Chance config (1 in 100 by default) on every growth tick where breeding did not succeed. Once it holds a weed the growth tick takes the "has a crop" branch and never calls attemptBreeding() again.
tips.g7.i5: Weed-EX in the middle stick prevents that, which is what makes a setup safe to leave running unattended.
tips.g7.i5w: spawnWeed() checks the stored Weed-EX before it plants anything and burns 5 points instead of placing the weed. How much a stick can hold is set by whoever fills it, and there are only two callers: the Weed-EX can passes addWeedEx(10, 90, 100) and a Crop Manager passes addWeedEx(75, 75, 150). So a full stick blocks 20 spawns when filled by hand and 30 when filled by the machine.
tips.g7.i6: A grown Necrobloom with a high growth stat spreads weeds itself. It has to be mature, have a growth stat above 8, and have resistance lower than that growth. With all three met it seeds weeds into the empty sticks around it, so keep it away from a breeding setup.
tips.g7.i6w: It lowers its weed-spreading threshold to a growth stat of 8, against the default of 24 that ordinary crops use. That is a stat on the 1…31 scale, not a growth stage. Even so it stays stricter than a real weed, which spreads from 50% growth with no stat conditions at all.
tips.g8.lead: Moving through a crop field can break the sticks and lose the plants on them.
tips.g8.i1: Do not sprint across a crop field. Sprinting can break a crop stick and destroy the plant on it, and the higher the tier the more often it happens. A resistance-31 plant is immune, and so is anything standing on tilled Fertilized Dirt, Enchanted Earth or Clean Dirt, which are registered as trample-proof.
tips.g8.i1w: Sprinting first rolls roughly 1 in 100 × 0.95^tier - about 1 in 95 for a tier 1 crop and 1 in 44 for a tier 16 one. Only if that hits does it roll again against resistance, breaking the stick when random(0…30) beats it. So the first figure is the ceiling, not the real rate: a tier 1 crop at resistance 20 actually breaks about 1 collision in 295.
tips.g8.i2: Do not land on crops from a height. Any drop over three quarters of a block can break the stick, and from 1.75 blocks it always does.
tips.g8.i2w: Landing triggers a check once the fall distance passes 0.75. The chance of breaking is the fall distance minus 0.75, so at 1.75 blocks the roll can no longer fail.
tips.g8.i3: Crouch to walk past crops that damage you. Ore berries, Bamboo, Thornvine and Cactus deal half a heart on contact. Sneaking skips the damage entirely.
tips.g8.i3w: The collision handler applies the crop's contact damage only when the entity is not sneaking. Those four crop types are the ones that declare a damage value above zero, all of them 1.0.
tips.g9.i1: Walking into a Goldfish plant makes it scream. A fully grown one plays at five times normal volume and a much lower pitch, so it carries a long way. A young one is quiet. Crouching skips it.
tips.g9.i1w: The collision handler skips the crop's hook entirely for a sneaking entity, and the scream only fires for players. Once mature it plays at volume 5.0 and pitch 0.5, against the 1.0 of an ordinary sound. Before maturity the volume is 3.0 scaled by growth and the pitch is 4.0 minus growth.
tips.g9.i2: It also screams at random while it is still growing, roughly once every 512 growth ticks per plant. A fully grown patch is silent unless stepped on.
tips.g9.i2w: The random scream is rolled from the growth tick, which only runs while the plant is actually growing: it draws a number under 512 and screams on exactly 42. That also means the random one is always the quiet version - the loud scream only comes from being stepped on. Two configs cover this: one silences crop sounds entirely, another leaves the random screams but stops the stepped-on one.
tips.g9.i3: Trollplant takes an absurd catalyst to duplicate. Five screws made of Fool's Ruby, an item with no other use. Two clay bricks or eight IC2 scrap work as well.
tips.g9.i3w: Its constructor registers three duplication catalysts: two vanilla bricks, five of the screwFoolsRuby ore dictionary entry, and eight IC2 scrap. Its flavour text is "Trololololol, lololol, lololol!".
tips.g10.lead: Not every crop can be bred, and not every crop can turn up by chance.
tips.g10.i1: Some crops belong to no pool at all. With two exceptions those can only come from their exact recipe; random crossing will never produce one. Gaia Wart and Primordial Berry have neither a pool nor a recipe, so the world is their only source.
tips.g10.i1w: In this pack ${Object.values(C).filter(c => !c.pools.length).length} of the ${Object.keys(C).length} crops are registered into no pool. The crop drawer lists this under Mutation pools.
tips.g10.i2: ${Object.values(C).filter(c => !MUT.some(m => m.out === c.id)).length} crops have no recipe at all: Wheat, Potato, Carrot, Dandelion, Poppy, Gaia Wart and Primordial Berry. Nothing breeds into them, so every chain starts from one of these. They do not all come the same way. ${Object.values(C).filter(c => !MUT.some(m => m.out === c.id) && c.pools.length).length} of them are in a mutation pool, so once you own anything you can still draw them out of a pair by luck - and a draw arrives with the parents' stats, which is the easy way to a maxed one. Gaia Wart and Primordial Berry are the exception, and with no pool to draw them from, cloning is the only way to improve those two.
tips.g10.i2w: Exactly ${Object.values(C).filter(c => !MUT.some(m => m.out === c.id)).length} crops never appear as the output of any recipe, so they can only come from world generation, mobs or loot. ${Object.values(C).filter(c => !MUT.some(m => m.out === c.id) && c.pools.length).length} of them are registered into at least one mutation pool; Gaia Wart and Primordial Berry are registered into none. Everything else in the pack can be bred if you can get hold of its parents.
tips.g10.i5: ${Object.values(C).filter(c => c.altSeed).length} of the ${Object.keys(C).length} crops can be planted from an ordinary item, with no breeding at all. Put the item on an empty crop stick and the crop is standing there at 1/1/1, already analysed - a crop that came out of a cross is not, and keeps its stats hidden until you scan it. That is how the ${Object.values(C).filter(c => !MUT.some(m => m.out === c.id)).length} crops with no recipe get in at all, and for the other ${Object.values(C).filter(c => c.altSeed && MUT.some(m => m.out === c.id)).length} it means breeding is the way to better stats rather than the only way in. The crop drawer says so under How to get it, and NEI lists the item under Alternate Seeds.
tips.g10.i5w: tryPlantSeed(ItemStack) asks CropRegistry.get() for the crop, and that falls through to fromAlternateSeed() for any stack that is not one of the mod's own seeds. When the item is not an ItemGenericSeed it builds new SeedStats(1, 1, 1, true), the fourth argument being the analysed flag; attemptBreeding() uses the same constructor for its result and passes false there. Planting checks the soil and nothing else: tryPlantSeed(ISeedData) calls isValidSoilForCrop(), which reads the block one below the stick, and no light, biome or under-block check runs before the crop is placed.
tips.g10.i3: A recipe with three or four parents needs that many grown crops around one stick. A stick has four sides, so four parents is the limit.
tips.g10.i3w: Only the four horizontal neighbours are read, and every one of a recipe's parents has to be standing there and grown enough at the same moment.
guide.note: Everything you need to get one crop to 31/31/31, and what to do with it once you have. The steps are the short route; the text around them explains why each one is there.
guide.b1: CropsNH grows materials. Metal, rubber, wood and many other items can be farmed instead of mined. All of it starts with crop sticks.
guide.b2: A crop stick holds one plant. While the stick is still empty you can right-click a second crop stick onto it, which makes a double crop stick. Only a double crop stick breeds. A single one never produces anything new.
guide.b3: Crop sticks are crafted in a crafting table from four Long Wood Sticks placed in a square, and one craft gives four sticks. A Long Wood Stick is itself a craft: two Wooden Sticks and a Hard Hammer in a row. So four crop sticks cost eight wooden sticks and a hammer you keep.
guide.b4: Once you finish the quest A Green Revolution, the Vending Machine sells them in bulk instead: 64 crop sticks for one log and 50 Adventure coins, and 128 Fertilizer for 25 Adventure coins, 5 Farmer coins, one spider eye, eight rotten flesh and 64 dirt. Coins come from quest rewards. That quest asks for 5 wheat seeds, 5 carrots and 5 potatoes, so it is worth doing early. Each trade then has a two-hour cooldown. Playing alone you get one purchase per trade in that window. On a server the limit is the number of your team members who are online.
guide.b5: You do not need CropsNH seeds to start. Right-click a Potato, a wheat seed or a sapling onto an empty crop stick and it becomes that CropsNH crop, at 1/1/1 and already analysed. About a hundred items work this way. NEI lists them under Alternate Seeds.
guide.b6: Every plant has three numbers: Growth, Gain and Resistance, each from 1 to 31. Growth sets how fast it grows. Gain sets how much one harvest gives. Resistance sets how well it resists disease, and whether the seed survives when you break the plant. A Plant Lens shows all three when you right-click a crop. The Plant Lens and the Spade are both CropsNH items with their own quests, and NEI has the recipes.
guide.b7: Every new plant rolls its three numbers again, and the roll can be negative. Fertilizer removes the negative half of the roll, so the numbers never go down. Right-click a crop stick with fertilizer to fill it. Bone meal works and needs nothing unlocked, so that is what the steps below use. The mod's own Fertilizer item is twenty times stronger per item, and once you have done A Green Revolution you can buy 128 of it from the Vending Machine at a time. Switch to it as soon as you can, because one Fertilizer fills a stick as far as twenty bone meal.
guide.b8: Fertilizer counts when it sits in the stick of the plant you are breeding from. Keep every plant you breed from fertilized.
guide.b9: A crop stick holds water as well as fertilizer, and the two do different jobs. Fertilizer protects the three numbers. Water only makes the plant grow faster, but that is most of the waiting in the loop below, so it is worth keeping full. A crop stick starts at 5 points of growth speed, full water adds 10 and full fertilizer adds another 10. Fill the water with a Watering Can from Extra Utilities: right-click the stick with it.
guide.title: Quick start
guide.lead: The goal is one crop at 31/31/31. Do this once and you never have to do it again.
guide.n1: Crop sticks - needed, the more the better. Craft them, or buy them from the Vending Machine and skip steps 1 and 2.
guide.n2: A Potato - needed. Any crop works, and these steps use a Potato.
guide.n3: Fertilizer - needed. Bone meal does the job and needs nothing unlocked.
guide.n4: A Plant Lens - needed. Without it you cannot read the numbers, and reading them is the whole loop.
guide.n5: A Watering Can from Extra Utilities - highly recommended. Water is most of the growth speed, and growth is most of the waiting.
guide.n6: A Spade - recommended. It takes the seed in the last step, and it tills the dirt in step 3.
guide.n7: A Hard Hammer - needed only if you craft the crop sticks yourself.
guide.s1: Craft four Long Wood Sticks. Each one is two Wooden Sticks and a Hard Hammer in a crafting table.
guide.s2: Put those four Long Wood Sticks in a square in a crafting table. You get four crop sticks.
guide.s3: Till a block of dirt and place one crop stick on it.
guide.s4: Right-click a ${cropLink("Potato")} onto the crop stick. You now have a Potato crop at 1/1/1.
guide.s5: Right-click the crop stick with bone meal to fertilize it, then right-click it with a Watering Can from Extra Utilities to fill its water.
guide.s6: Wait until the Potato is at least 80% grown. A Plant Lens shows the growth progress.
guide.s7: Place a double crop stick on each of the four blocks north, south, east and west of the Potato. Each one breeds on its own, so you get four tries per round instead of one.
guide.s8: Wait. A copy of the Potato grows on each double crop stick. Because the parent had fertilizer, no copy is worse than the parent: each number stays the same or goes up by as much as 4.
guide.s9: Right-click every plant with a Plant Lens to read the numbers.
guide.s10: Pick the plant with the highest numbers. Break everything else.
guide.s11: Fertilize and water the stick of the plant you kept, then repeat from step 7. Keep going until a plant shows 31/31/31.
guide.s12: Once that plant is 31/31/31 and fully grown, right-click it with a Spade. You get a seed carrying the same numbers, and the plant stays standing.
guide.a1: A new plant gets its three numbers from the plants it grew from, never from what it turns out to be. Grow it from one plant and it gets that plant's numbers. Grow it from two and it gets their average.
guide.a2: A fertilized 31/31/31 plant breeds into another 31/31/31 plant. If the fertilizer runs out, the new plant can come out at 29 or 30.
guide.a3: A double crop stick can grow three different things. Half the time it grows a copy of one of the plants beside it.
guide.a4: A copy. The plants next to the stick are all the same species, so a copy is all you can get. This is the loop above.
guide.a5: A recipe. Some pairs have a fixed result. A ${cropLink("Carrot")} next to a ${cropLink("Potato")} gives ${cropLink("SugarCane")} half the time, a Carrot a quarter of the time and a Potato the last quarter. No other crop can come out of that pair.
guide.a6: A pool mutation. Every crop carries a few tags, called breeding pools. When a pair fits no recipe, the game gives you a random crop that carries one of the parents' tags.
guide.a7: Potato carries three tags: ${poolLink("root")}, ${poolLink("yellow")} and ${poolLink("food")}. Click any of them to see every crop it holds. Plant two Potatoes one block apart with a double crop stick in the gap and the stick draws from all ${GUIDE_POOL_UNION} crops carrying any of those tags. That half is spread across the whole pool, so the smaller the pool, the better your odds for any one crop. Two crops that share only Root draw from ${POOLM.root.length}, which is ${pct(0.5 / POOLM.root.length)} each.
guide.a8: Tick off the crops you have in the list on the left. <button class="goview" type="button" data-goview="ready">Ready</button> lists recipes you can run now. <button class="goview" type="button" data-goview="near">One parent short</button> lists recipes that are missing one parent. <button class="goview" type="button" data-goview="pool">Pool roulette</button> shows the odds for any pair.
guide.seeAll: See every result for two Potatoes
tips.note: Everything here was read out of the pack's own code rather than collected from experience, so it should hold exactly. Hover why on any line to see where it comes from.
rail.markTitle: needs a specific under block, see the crop for which one
rail.markBreeder: Every recipe for this crop runs only in the Crop Breeder, and no pool holds it - a crop stick will never produce it
rail.markNone: No recipe and no pool. Nothing breeds this crop, on a stick or in the machine
warn.noStorageFramed: This browser will not let the page store anything, so your ticks disappear on reload. Press Copy and keep the text somewhere before you close the tab.
warn.noStorage: This browser will not let the page store anything, so your ticks disappear on reload. Take a copy with Download file or Copy before you close it.
chip.onlyTitle: This recipe only runs in the Crop Breeder machine, never on a crop stick
tips.g10.i4: A recipe marked only in Crop Breeder never fires on a crop stick. The mark is on the recipe, not on the crop, so on its own it does not mean the crop is out of reach. In this pack it works out that way anyway: ${MUT.filter(m => m.machineOnly).length} recipes carry the mark, and for ${MUT.filter(m => m.machineOnly && !MUT.some(x => x.out === m.out && !x.machineOnly) && !C[m.out].pools.length).length} of them the crop has no other recipe and belongs to no pool, so the machine really is its only source.
tips.g10.i4w: machineOnly() attaches a MachineOnlyBreedingRequirement, whose canBreed() returns false without looking at anything. Requirements are filtered by interface: the crop stick asks only those implementing IWorldBreedingRequirement and the machine only IMachineBreedingRequirement, and this one implements the first alone, so the machine never sees it. On a stick the recipe fails its conditions like any other, which means that half of the attempt falls back to a pool draw.
tips.g12.h: Oil Berry at MV when everything is 31/31/31
tips.g12.lead: Good seeds are the problem here, and one Sugar Cane is the whole fix.
tips.g12.i1: An MV Crop Breeder will not make ${nm("OilBerry")} from two 31/31/31 parents, and it reports no error. The recipe consumes ${144 * C.OilBerry.tier} L of enriched fertilizer for the tier of the output, plus 72 L for each point of stat on it. At 31/31/31 that is ${144 * C.OilBerry.tier + 72 * 93} L against a 6400 L tank. The output takes the average of its two parents, so the pair only has to come in under ${Math.floor((6400 - 144 * C.OilBerry.tier) / 72)} points and only one of them has to drop.
tips.g12.i1w: MTECropBreeder.getFluidAmount() is max(1, tier × 144) + max(1, (growth + gain + resistance) × 72), in litres of enriched fertilizer, the only fluid in ALLOWED_LIQUID_FERTILIZER and registered there at a multiplier of 1. getCustomFluidCapacity() divides GregTech's getCapacityForTier() by five below tier 5, which gives 3200 L at LV, 6400 L at MV and 12800 L at HV. checkRecipe() compares the cost against the fluid in the tank and moves on to the next recipe when it does not fit, so nothing is reported. getNewSeedStats() adds each stat over the recipe's parents and divides by their count with integer division, so the machine rolls nothing.
tips.g12.i2: Stand a 1/1/1 ${nm("SugarCane")} and your 31/31/31 ${nm("Withereed")} either side of a double crop stick, on stone with a block of coal under the stick. The two share only reed, which holds ${POOLM.reed.length} crops, and a pool draw averages every parent in the pool it drew from, so it produces a ${nm("Withereed")} at 16/16/16. That ground rejects the rest of the pool, so the only crop that ever appears on the stick is a ${nm("Withereed")}: at 31 from a copy, at 16 from a draw. Read them with a Plant Lens, take the low one off with a Spade, and pair it with the ${nm("SoulSandLily")} you already have. 16 and 31 average to 23/23/23, which is 69 points.
tips.g12.i2w: getBreedingResult() filters the neighbours differently on its two halves. The cloning half keeps only those whose crop equals the one it picked, so a ${nm("SugarCane")} standing next to a ${nm("Withereed")} has no effect on a ${nm("Withereed")} copy. The pool half keeps every neighbour that is a member of the drawn pool, and both of these are in reed, so variateStat() averages 31 and 1 into 16. The draw is half of every attempt and reed has ${POOLM.reed.length} members, which puts ${nm("Withereed")} at ${pct(0.5 / POOLM.reed.length)} per attempt. attemptBreeding() then throws away any result that fails isValidSoilForCrop() or wouldCropBeAbleToGrow() on the breeding stick: ${nm("Blazereed")} needs netherrack, ${nm("SugarCane")} and ${nm("StickyCane")} need sand or dirt, and ${nm("Diareed")} needs diamond rather than coal under the stone.
tips.g12.i3: Keep two seeds of each parent. The recipe needs 120 EU/t for 520 ticks, which an MV machine supplies, but an MV Crop Breeder succeeds 50% of the time and a failed attempt still consumes one seed of each parent and the full fluid cost.
tips.g12.i3w: CropOilBerry.getMachineBreedingRecipeTier() returns 2, and setBreedingMachineRecipeTier() turns that into GTValues.VP[2] for the voltage and 400 × 1.3^(tier - 1) for the duration. getOutputChance() is min(100, 40 + (tier - 1) × 10), so 40% at LV, 50% at MV and 60% at HV. checkRecipe() subtracts the fluid and one of each parent stack before it rolls against that chance, so a failed attempt costs the same as a successful one. MutationLoader registers the recipe as new CropMutation(OilBerry, SoulSandLily, Withereed).machineOnly().
app.lead: Notes about the tool rather than about the mod. Nothing here needs a source.
app.i1: Every crop name on this page opens a panel. Soil, under block, light, the pools it sits in, every recipe that makes it and everything it is a parent for.
app.i2: Type in the search box and press Enter to tick the top match and clear the box, so a handful of seeds goes in without touching the mouse.
app.i3: Pool roulette remembers the last ten pairs you looked at and offers the five most recent under the pickers, which beats rebuilding a pair from two dropdowns every time.
app.i4: The star on a pair keeps it in a Saved row of its own, so the two or three pairs a plot is built around stay put while Recent rolls over.
app.i5: Click a card to mark what you are building. It gets a green edge and moves to the front of the grid, which is the difference between glancing at a second monitor and reading it.
app.i6: Manage list, under the seed list, copies your ticks out as text and back in - the way to move a list between this page and an offline copy, or to keep a backup.
app.i7: The address bar follows what you are looking at, so a link you send opens on the same tab, the same pair and the same open panel, and F5 keeps you where you were.
app.i8: The language picker sits at the top right and carries your place across, so switching does not send you back to the first tab.
app.i9: Your ticks never leave the browser. The page makes no requests to anywhere, which also means it works with the network off and that each copy keeps its own list.
about.note: What this tool is, how to work it, and where its numbers come from. The Tips & tricks tab is the other half: that one is about the mod, and every line in it names the method it was read from.
foot.short: A planner for CropsNH breeding in GregTech: New Horizons, read out of the mod's own code rather than from a wiki. Your ticks stay in this browser and the page works offline.
tips.g4.i6: Once a plant is grown, the block under it can be taken away. The under block is checked when something is planted and on every growth tick, and a mature plant has no growth ticks left to fail - so one block can serve a whole setup. Grow the parent on it, break it out from underneath, and put it under the breeding stick, which is where the copy has to be able to land. Diareed and its block of diamond is the case where this is worth the walk, but it applies to all ${Object.values(C).filter(c => c.subsoil.length).length} crops marked ◆. Put the block back before you pick the crop: harvesting checks the requirements again.
tips.g4.i6w: canGrow() returns false for a mature plant before looking at any requirement, so there is nothing left for a missing sub-soil to stop. Nothing removes the plant either - a stick only breaks itself through onInvalidSoilDetected(), which the block calls after reading y - 1 against the crop's soil list, while the sub-soil sits at y - 2 and is not part of that check. canCross() asks only for a crop, no weed, and growth past the crossing threshold, so the stripped parent still counts as a parent. canHarvest() does re-run the requirements, which is why the block has to be back for the harvest.
drawer.likesNote: biome tags, not a requirement - see Tips & tricks
tips.g5.i7: The Likes line in NEI is a list of biome tags, and matching them is the largest single bonus in the game. Match one and the crop gets +14 Nutrient Score, match two and it gets +28 - more than half the ceiling of 55. A third tag does nothing, the count is capped at two. It also replaces the wet-biome bonus rather than adding to it, so a crop in a biome it likes stops caring how damp the place is. The crop panel on this page lists the tags next to the growth time.
tips.g5.i7w: The tile counts how many of getLikedBiomeTags() appear in the biome's own BiomeDictionary types, clamps that count to 2, and hands it to getNutrientsPerCycle(). There the score ends with max(humidityBonus, matched × 14), where the humidity bonus is (rainfall - 0.5) ÷ 0.3 clamped to 0…1 and multiplied by 14. Which is why the two never stack and why 28 is the most a biome can ever be worth.
tips.g5.i8: Two ways to find out whether a spot is any good, neither of them inside CropsNH. A Portable Scanner used on a crop stick prints the Nutrient Score out of the score that crop needs - it works on an empty stick too, so you can test a place before planting. Nature's Compass lists the tags of every biome as subtext and can sort biomes by tag, which is the way to find somewhere your crop likes. In the Industrial Farm the question goes away: an Environmental Module carries one tag and is added on top of whatever the biome already has, so two of them reach the +28 anywhere.
tips.g5.i8w: The scanner readout comes from BlockScanningEventHandler, which calls getPlantLensStatus() and then getNutrientScore(), formatted through the same scanner.6 string the Industrial Farm uses. MTEIndustrialFarm builds a set from BiomeDictionary.getTypesForBiome() at its own position, then adds the tag of every ItemEnvironmentalModule in its slots before counting matches, so modules top the biome up rather than replace it. The tags themselves are Forge's, which is why a biome's list belongs to the mod that added it and CropsNH never prints it.
tag.intro: One biome tag. Matching it is worth +14 Nutrient Score to a crop that likes it, and two matched tags are worth +28.
tag.noBiomes: No biome in this pack carries it.
biome.intro: What this biome is worth to a crop. Two matched tags are the cap, a third adds nothing.
biomes.note: Which biome to build in. The tags belong to Forge rather than to CropsNH, so this table is read from Minecraft itself and from the mods that add biomes - Biomes O' Plenty, Twilight Forest, RWG and Thaumcraft. A crop matching two of a biome's tags gets +28 Nutrient Score, more than half the ceiling of 55.
about.biomeData: One table is not from CropsNH. Biome tags belong to Forge, and each biome is registered by whichever mod added it, so the Biomes tab is read out of Minecraft itself and out of Biomes O' Plenty, Twilight Forest, RWG and Thaumcraft - the mods in this pack that register any. Tags and rainfall are then taken from the game's own biome dump, because three of Forge's tags are compounds that expand on the way in: a biome registered as Water answers Ocean and River, and Water is what a reading of the registration alone would have kept. A mod that adds biomes without registering tags simply will not appear.
drawer.whereFull: The full +28 Nutrient Score - two of its tags match:
drawer.whereNoneFull: No biome in this pack carries two of its tags, so +14 is the most it can get from a biome.
drawer.whereOneTag: It likes a single tag, so a biome can never be worth more than +14 to it.
app.i10: A crop's Likes tags are links, and the panel names the biomes worth +28 to it and the ones worth +14. The Biomes tab goes the other way: search a place by name or by tag and see what is worth growing there.
tips.g6.i3: Wheat, Potato, Carrot, Dandelion and Poppy have no recipe, and they do not need one. A crop that comes out of a pool draw takes its stats from the two parents beside the stick, not from whatever it turns out to be. So put two 31/31/31 parents that share a pool with Carrot around a stick, and the Carrot that eventually appears is already 31/31/31. Pick the parents by the smallest pool they share. Salty Root + Turnip share only root, which holds ${POOLM.root.length} crops, so each of them comes up ${pct(0.5 / POOLM.root.length)} of the time. A pair whose only shared pool is food is spread over ${POOLM.food.length} crops instead, which is ${pct(0.5 / POOLM.food.length)}. Gaia Wart and Primordial Berry are in no pool at all, so those two really do have to be cloned up one plant at a time.
tips.g6.i3w: attemptBreeding() hands its neighbour list to getBreedingResult(), which filters that same list in place - for a pool draw it removes every neighbour whose crop the matched pool does not contain. What is left is mapped to its seeds and passed to variateStat() once per stat, and the fertiliser flag is an allMatch over the same list. Nothing along that path reads the result, which is why the result's own stats never enter into it.
tips.g5.i9: Fertiliser items are not all worth the same. Bone Meal adds 5 points, Forestry's Fertilizer Compound adds 25, Forestry's Bio Fertilizer adds 50, and this mod's own Fertilizer fills the tank with a single item. The tank stops at 100 and the rest of the item is thrown away, so keep the strong ones for a tank that is nearly empty.
tips.g5.i9w: FertilizerLoader.registerItemFertilizers() registers the potencies: bone meal 5, Forestry's fertilizerCompound 25, fertilizerBio 50, and CropsNH's own fertiliser 100. A right click calls addFertilizer(potency, max(90, 100 - potency), 100), which does nothing while the store is above that threshold and otherwise clamps the sum to 100.
tips.g5.i10: The Crop Manager waters, fertilises and harvests a whole field on its own. It is a single-block machine from this mod, and its range grows with its tier: 5 blocks sideways at LV, 2 more for every tier above that, and 2 blocks up and down. When a machine fills them, the tanks in a stick hold 200 instead of 100. That does not raise the Nutrient Score, it only doubles how long the field runs without you.
tips.g5.i10w: MTECropManager is registered from LV up to UMV. getHorizontalRadius() returns 3 + 2 × tier and the vertical radius is 2. It applies water and fertiliser with a cap of 200, while getNutrientsPerCycle() reads both through min(100, …), so anything above 100 is stored but never counted.
tips.g5.i11: Underground, watering is not enough on its own. A crop that cannot see the sky loses the 2 points for sky access, and no rain reaches it, so the tank only ever holds what you carry down. With full water and a biome that adds nothing, the score stops at 15, and fertiliser is what takes it to 25. The biome itself still counts down there, because the score reads it from the column and never looks at the height: a cave under a biome the crop likes is worth the same +28 as the surface.
tips.g5.i11w: getNutrientScore() adds 2 when World.canBlockSeeTheSky() is true for the block above the stick, and the growth tick only refills water when World.isRainingAt() is true, which never happens below ground. The biome comes from getBiomeGenForCoordsBody(x, z), which takes no y coordinate at all.
tips.g6.i4: A high growth stat makes a plant grow more than five times faster. Growth speed starts at 6 plus the growth stat, so a plant with growth 1 starts at 7 and one with growth 31 starts at 37. Water, fertiliser and the biome only add or subtract a percentage of that number, which is why this stat is worth more than all of them together.
tips.g6.i4w: getGrowthRate() builds its base as BASE_GROWTH_SPEED + growth, where BASE_GROWTH_SPEED is 6, then scales that base by the percentage it gets from comparing score × 5 with tier × 10. The best that percentage can ever do is multiply by 3.65, which needs a perfect score of 55 on a tier 1 crop, while the stat alone spans 7 to 37.
tips.g11.lead: Six items you can hold. One of them changes how seeds come off a plant.
tips.g11.i1: A spade in your hand adds a seed to every harvest, and the plant stays standing. Right-click a grown crop the way you always do: you get the produce, plus a seed carrying that plant's exact stats, and the plant drops back to zero growth and grows again. Bare-handed there is no seed at harvest at all, and the only way to one is breaking the plant. The plain Spade drops a single seed on a roll against resistance, so 31 gives one every time; the Reinforced Spade skips the roll entirely and drops resistance ÷ 10 of them, which is three or four from a 31/31/31 plant. Neither ever wears out.
tips.g11.i1w: ItemSpadeNH implements IHarvestDropModifier, and doPlayerHarvest(player, breakCrop) calls modifyCropDrops() on the held item right after harvest(). A right click passes breakCrop = false, so the tile only sets growthProgress = 0 and keeps the plant; the seed a bare hand can get sits on the other branch, which runs only when that flag is set. ItemSpade.addSeedDrop() takes getSeedDrop(), gated on passesResistanceCheck(), namely resistance > random(0…30). ItemReinforcedSpade.addSeedDrop() takes getSeedStack() with no roll at all and sets the stack size to resistance / 10, adding one more with probability (resistance mod 10) / 10. Both constructors call setMaxDamage(0), which in 1.7.10 means the item cannot be damaged.
tips.g11.i2: Run a Plant Lens over the plant before you take seeds off it. The lens marks the plant analysed for good, and every seed taken afterwards comes out analysed too, so the copies never need scanning.
tips.g11.i2w: ItemPlantLens.onRightClick() calls ISeedData.setAnalyzed(true), and SeedData.setAnalyzed() rebuilds the cached ItemStack out of the crop and the stats rather than flipping a flag on the tile. getSeedStack() hands back a copy of that same stack, so the flag travels with the seed.
tips.g11.i3: The Plant Lens also answers why a plant is standing still. Besides the stats it prints how much fertiliser, water and Weed-EX is left in the stick, whether the plant is sick, and every growth requirement that is failing right now, in red. It is the fastest way to tell an empty tank from a missing block.
tips.g11.i3w: getPlantLensStatus() writes one line for the three stores, one for weeds, the crop name coloured by its rarity, the stats when the seed is analysed, a sick warning, and then one red line per entry of failedChecks. That list is filled by areGrowthRequirementsMet(), which walks every IWorldGrowthRequirement the crop declares.
tips.g11.i4: ${Object.values(C).filter(c => c.machineGrow).length} crops grow to full on an ordinary crop stick and cannot be harvested by hand. They are not stuck: a spade takes a seed off them anyway. Right-click drops the seed and resets the growth, left-click drops it and clears the stick. Below resistance 31 that is a gamble worth knowing about, because the growth is reset whether the seed came out or not. The produce still needs the Industrial Farm. The crop drawer says so under Growing conditions.
tips.g11.i4w: Those crops attach a MachineOnlyGrowthRequirement, whose canGrow() always returns false while its onlyPreventsHarvest() returns true, so growth runs to the end and only canHarvest() refuses. The spade's own doWork() fires in exactly that gap: mature, growth requirements met, and canHarvest() false. It drops the seed and then runs clear() on a left click or setGrowthProgress(0) on a right one, neither of them conditional on the seed having appeared. The requirement implements IWorldGrowthRequirement alone, which is why the Industrial Farm never sees it.
tips.g11.i5: A spade is also a hoe, and the only one that goes back. It turns grass, dirt and mycelium into farmland, and farmland back into dirt. The farmland list and the dirt/grass list share no block at all, so that one tool is how a spot moves from either to the other without carrying blocks around.
tips.g11.i5w: ItemSpadeNH.TILLABLE_BLOCKS maps grass, dirt and mycelium to farmland, and farmland to dirt. onItemUse() posts Forge's UseHoeEvent first, then swaps the block when the map has an entry for it and the space above is empty.
tips.g11.i6: Plant Cure and the Weed-EX can are small and single-purpose. Plant Cure clears a sick plant and tops the stick's fertiliser up to 25, and it spends one of its 100 uses only when there was something to cure. The Weed-EX can adds 10 to the stick's store with a ceiling of 100, over 75 uses, and does nothing at all while the store is already above 90.
tips.g11.i6w: ItemPlantCure.onRightClick() calls cureDisease() and, only when that returns true, addFertilizer(25, 25, 25) followed by one point of damage; the constructor sets setMaxDamage(100). ItemWeedEX.onRightClick() calls addWeedEx(10, 90, 100) and its constructor sets setMaxDamage(75). addWeedEx(potency, threshold, max) returns false while the store is above the threshold, and otherwise raises it by the potency and clamps to the max.
drawer.machineGrow: Only the Industrial Farm can harvest this. It grows to full on an ordinary crop stick, but nothing comes off it by hand. A spade still takes a seed.
tips.g11.i7: Hold sneak while you place a crop stick and the double one goes down in a single click. Placing it normally and then right-clicking it again with sticks in hand gets you the same thing in two. The shortcut takes two sticks out of the stack at once, and with only one left in hand it quietly places an ordinary single stick instead - worth a glance at the stack before you work your way along a row.
tips.g11.i7w: ItemCropSticks.onItemUse() builds one flag out of player.isSneaking() and either creative mode or stackSize >= 2. With the flag set it places the block, subtracts 2 from the stack rather than 1, then calls setCrossCrop(true) on the tile it has just created. A stack of one fails the second half of that test, so the flag stays false and the click places an ordinary stick. The two-click route is onRightClick(), which upgrades a stick that is already standing for one more and is the only one of the two that plays the cross-crop sound.
tips.g8.i4: As of 2.0.108 boots do the same job as crouching, without the crouching. Hazmat gear makes you immune outright: the plain sort wears out slowly doing it, about a point of durability every hundred brushes, and the powered sort never takes a scratch. Plain Leather Boots are the cheap version and take roughly three quarters of the damage away. The same protection shortens Necrobloom's poison by the same fraction, and full cover stops it entirely. NEI lists every pair that counts under Boot Protection, which is worth a look because the list is long and depends on what the pack has loaded.
tips.g8.i4w: BootProtectionRegistry.FULL_PROTECTION is 1.0, and BootProtectionLoader states its own rule in a comment: hazmat that is not electric gives immunity but takes damage, hazmat that is electric or comes with full space suit protection gives immunity and takes none. Below full protection TileEntityCropSticks.onEntityCollision() swaps the crop's damage for 0.01 with a probability equal to the protection value; the comment there explains this as working around the hit immunity window rather than scaling damage directly. Leather boots are registered at FULL_PROTECTION × 0.75 whenever IC2 is loaded, which in this pack it always is. The wear is DamageBootProtectionHandler(1, 100, …) against DAMAGE_CHANCE_MAX = 10000, so one point of durability on 1% of collisions, while registerFullProtectionHandler never touches it. CropNecrobloom.onEntityCollision() multiplies the poison duration by 1 - protection / FULL_PROTECTION and returns early at full protection. Sneaking still skips the whole hook before any of this is asked.
